keep: He did not invent the light bulb. He invented the room where a lamp, a station and a meter got built together.
lede: He went to school only briefly, and in later life was almost totally deaf. He did not invent the light bulb, and the line about ten thousand ways that won't work is not his. What he built was a laboratory that promised a minor invention every ten days.
copy: Edison was born in Milan, Ohio, on 11 February 1847. He went to school only briefly in Port Huron, Michigan, and was taught mostly at home by his mother. His 1910 authorised biography says his deafness began with a conductor boxing his ears after a chemistry fire in a baggage car; the story has rivals. He worked as a telegraph operator across the Midwest and joined Western Union in Boston in 1868. His first two patents came that year: a printing telegraph that was used for stock quotations, and a vote recorder the state legislature would not buy. In April 1876 he opened a laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, with two experimenters and three machinists. He was twenty-nine and already held a hundred patents. The plan, in his words, was a minor invention every ten days and a big thing every six months or so. The phonograph came in December 1877.

Electric light was older than he was. Humphry Davy made a platinum strip glow in 1802, and Joseph Swan was working on carbon lamps long before Menlo Park was. In 1879 Edison bought the rights to a Canadian patent of 1874 held by Henry Woodward and Mathew Evans. What he and his staff went after was a filament of high resistance, so that a whole district of lamps could run on little current. The money came first: the Edison Electric Light Company was incorporated on 16 October 1878 by investors around Western Union and Drexel, Morgan, and he assigned it his lighting patents for $30,000 plus stock and royalties. On 22 October 1879 the first high-resistance carbon filament worked. Patent 223,898, granted on 27 January 1880, does not claim a bulb. Its first claim is a filament of carbon of high resistance. On 4 September 1882 the Pearl Street station in Manhattan switched on. Its six dynamos could feed 7,200 lamps, and on the first day there were about 400.

The rest of the record is less tidy. In the second half of 1888 he ran electrocution experiments on dogs and other animals with Arthur Kennelly and Harold Brown, and his company branded Westinghouse's alternating current the executioner's current. On 23 July 1889 he testified on electrocution in the suit brought for William Kemmler, the first person sentenced to die that way. He then sank about $2.5 million of his own money into milling low-grade iron ore. When it failed, he said it was all gone but they had had a hell of a good time spending it. Near-total deafness did not stop him choosing every artist the phonograph company recorded, a policy his own papers call disastrous; the business was abandoned in 1929. And the line about failure is a retelling. In the 1910 biography his associate Walter Mallory remembers him, after more than nine thousand experiments on a storage battery, saying he had gotten a lot of results: he knew several thousand things that would not work. There is no ten thousand in it, and no "I have not failed". He left 1,093 US patents.

bio.why: Israel directs the Thomas A. Edison Papers at Rutgers, so this is the life written from inside the archive, and it treats the laboratory as the invention. That is also its limit; Mark Essig's Edison and the Electric Chair (2003) is the book from outside it on 1888 and 1889, unread here. The 1910 life by Dyer and Martin is free on Project Gutenberg and is where most of the legends start.

contested: How much of the Edison legend is Edison's. The 1910 biography was authorised and leans on his own recollections, forty years after the events; it gives the boxed ears as the direct cause of his deafness. Paul Israel, as Howard Markel reported for PBS NewsHour in 2018, points instead to ear infections and perhaps scarlet fever. The vote recorder has two versions too: the Edison Papers say a state legislature would not buy it, and the 1910 life sets it before a committee in Washington. On the lamp, the dispute is about what counts as inventing. Swan in Britain had begun on carbon lamps earlier and took a British patent in 1880; Edison's case rests on the high-resistance filament and the system around it, which is what his patent claims. On the electric chair the Edison Papers' own essay is the fullest account opened here. It says Edison was an important witness in the Kemmler suit, that the experiments were prompted by the SPCA and a state commission on humane execution, and that the Edison lighting interests, but not Edison himself, obtained the Westinghouse dynamo used. That essay is written by the Papers, which Israel directs. Essig (2003) and Richard Moran's Executioner's Current (2002) are the outside accounts, and this entry has not opened either.

US patent for an electric lamp with a high-resistance carbon filament, filed 4 November 1879 and granted 27 January 1880: Google Patents, US223898A
Lamps Pearl Street's six dynamos could supply, and lamps lit on the first day, 4 September 1882 (some 85 customers): ETHW, 'Milestones: Pearl Street Station, 1882' (IEEE History Center)
